wine.name: Grosset Polish Hill Riesling
wine.grapes: Riesling alone, from the Polish Hill River locality of the valley.
wine.sites: The house's own vineyard in the Polish Hill River locality, east of Sevenhill, at about 460 to 480 metres: silt and shallow shale over a thin crust of clay and gravel on blue slate, a hard rock site of small bunches and berries.
wine.making: The grapes are pressed gently and the free run juice is settled cold and fermented with neutral yeast for about two weeks in temperature controlled stainless steel, in batches by clone and vine age, before it is blended and bottled young. No oak and no malolactic fermentation; the wine has been sealed under screwcap since the 2000 vintage.
wine.glass: Lime juice and lime zest, lemon blossom and green apple over a crushed slate note; bone dry and light in body, with high, tight acidity and a long, linear finish. Age brings toast and a honeyed edge to the lime.
wine.ageing: Tight and reserved when young, it opens slowly and keeps for a decade and more, longer and more austere than the house's Springvale.
wine.serve: 8 to 10 degrees Celsius; no need to decant; a white wine glass, as an aperitif or with crab or grilled fish.

label.means: The locality east of Sevenhill where the vineyard lies; a local name, not a legal subregion.
The geographical indication; at least 85 per cent of the wine must come from it.
The variety named on the label; at least 85 per cent of the wine must be made from it.

records.table: Grosset Polish Hill is a bone dry Clare Valley Riesling from shallow shale over blue slate in the Polish Hill River locality: lime, lemon blossom and a stony edge on tight, high acidity. It opens more slowly than the house's Springvale, so give it years.
records.story: Polish Hill River took its name from settlers: in 1856 the ship August brought more than a hundred Polish migrants to South Australia, and the largest group farmed by the Hill River east of Sevenhill, which came to be called Polish Hill River. In 1981 the founder, a young winemaker, set up his own winery at Auburn, at the southern end of the valley, in a building that the house says had served early in the twentieth century as a butter and ice factory. His first wines that year included two dry Rieslings, one from Watervale and one from Polish Hill, and the house has made both in every vintage since. It came to farm its own vineyard at Polish Hill, a hard rock site of shale over slate, certified organic and biodynamic by its own account. In 2000 the house led a group of fourteen Clare producers who bottled their Riesling under screwcap together, so that no one maker carried alone the risk of a closure many buyers then distrusted; the valley's Riesling has been sealed that way since. Polish Hill shows a sommelier what a site does to Riesling: beside the house's Watervale wine, Springvale, it is tighter, stonier and slower to open.

others.name: Springvale Riesling
others.note: The house's Watervale Riesling from limestone, more open, with lime blossom to the fore, and approachable earlier than Polish Hill.

others.name: Gaia
others.note: A blend of Cabernet Sauvignon and Cabernet Franc from the house's Gaia vineyard high in the valley.

traps: Polish Hill River and Watervale are localities of the Clare Valley; the region has no legally defined subregions, so the geographical indication on the label is Clare Valley.
Clare dry Riesling is fully dry: expecting residual sugar is the standard error.
Polish Hill and Springvale are two sites of one house, not two tiers of quality.

cards.front: Grosset Polish Hill: what lies beneath the vineyard?
cards.back: Silt and shallow shale over a thin crust of clay and gravel, on blue slate.

questions.q: A guest compares Grosset's two Clare Rieslings and asks why Polish Hill is the tighter and slower of the pair. Which reason fits?
opts: Shallow shale over slate on a hard rock site
Late picking with a touch of noble rot
Fermentation and ageing in old oak casks
Fruit from the warm, fertile valley floor
questions.exp: The vineyard is shallow shale and silt over blue slate, where the vines struggle and give small berries; the wine sees no oak at all, so the cask answer is wrong.

questions.q: Grosset led fourteen Clare producers in one change for the 2000 vintage. What did they change?
opts: The closure, from cork to screwcap
The harvest, to picking by night
questions.exp: The fourteen bottled their 2000 Riesling under screwcap together so no single maker bore the risk; the region has no legal subregions to name on a label.

report: The house's vineyard page, read through a search summary, says the Polish Hill site was selected and planted by the house in 1996, yet the wine has been made since 1981, so earlier vintages must have drawn on other Polish Hill fruit; the record names no planting year and the checker may settle it.

The making rests on Liberty Wines (pressing, free run, neutral yeast, two weeks in stainless steel) and a retailer's note (cold settling, no oak, no malolactic); one note says no pressings are used and another names a pneumatic press, so the record says pressed gently and free run.
The fourteen producers of 2000 rest on the Clare Valley Wine and Grape Association's page and several secondary accounts; one account says thirteen.

The library's trap for Jim Barry Wines calls Watervale a Clare subregion, and Grosset's library trap calls Polish Hill and Watervale subregions; the Clare Valley Wine and Grape Association says the region has no legally defined subregions and Wine Australia's register lists none, so the record calls them localities.
The Polish settlers of 1856 rest on the South Australian history hub and the Clare museum's page.
The founder is living and is not named. No swap proposed.

wine.name: The Armagh Shiraz
wine.grapes: Shiraz alone, from the Armagh vineyard.
wine.sites: The Armagh vineyard, by the hamlet of Armagh near the town of Clare, on land the founder bought in 1964; its Shiraz was planted in the late 1960s, by the house's story from cuttings taken at Wendouree.
wine.making: Fermented in small open fermenters with heading down boards, pumped over and racked and returned for colour and flavour, then pressed and matured in hogsheads and barriques for well over a year. The first vintages were fermented in stainless steel and aged in new American oak; American oak was later reduced and then given up for French.
wine.glass: Blackberry, mulberry and dark chocolate over mint and black pepper; full bodied and dense, with ripe, fine grained tannin, fresh acidity and a long, warm finish.
wine.ageing: Dense and closed for its first years, it wants a decade in a strong vintage and keeps for twenty years and more.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for an hour or two, an old one gently off its sediment; a large red wine glass.

label.means: The vineyard's name, taken from the hamlet of Armagh near Clare.
The geographical indication; at least 85 per cent of the wine must come from it.
The Australian name for Syrah, the one variety in the bottle.

records.table: Jim Barry Wines makes The Armagh from Shiraz the founder planted by the hamlet of Armagh in the late 1960s, first bottled under that name from the 1985 vintage. It is blackberry, dark chocolate and mint in a dense, full red, so decant it and use a large glass.
records.story: Jim Barry, who died in 2004 at the age of seventy nine, graduated from Roseworthy College in 1947 and went to the Clarevale co-operative, by most accounts the first qualified winemaker the Clare Valley had. In 1959 he and his wife bought their first property and founded Jim Barry Wines. In 1964 he bought land near the hamlet of Armagh, planting Cabernet Sauvignon and Malbec first and Shiraz at the end of the decade, from cuttings the house says came from the old vines of Wendouree. For years that Shiraz went into a port style blend. In 1985, the year the founder retired and his son took charge, the family kept the vineyard's Shiraz apart, and that vintage, launched in 1989, became the first The Armagh. In 1986 the family bought the Florita vineyard at Watervale from Lindemans, once the source of Leo Buring's Rieslings, and gave the house its Riesling to match the red. Over the years The Armagh moved from new American oak to French. In 2020 its 2016 vintage was offered through La Place de Bordeaux, the merchant system of Bordeaux, the first Australian Shiraz so sold. For a sommelier it is the answer to anyone who thinks Clare makes only Riesling.

others.name: The Florita Riesling
others.note: Dry Riesling from the Watervale vineyard the family bought from Lindemans in 1986, once a source of Leo Buring's Rieslings.

others.name: The McRae Wood Shiraz
others.note: The house's other single vineyard Shiraz, the step below The Armagh.

traps: The Armagh names a hamlet and a vineyard in the Clare Valley; nothing in the bottle comes from the Irish county.
Clare is not only a white region: The Armagh is dense, long lived Shiraz from the same valley as the house's Florita Riesling.
Watervale is a locality of the Clare Valley, not a separate geographical indication.

questions.q: A guest asks how the making of The Armagh Shiraz has changed since its first vintages. Which change is right?
opts: New American oak gave way to French oak
French barrels gave way to concrete eggs
Open fermenters gave way to clay amphorae

questions.exp: The early vintages were aged in new American oak, which was reduced and later given up for French; the wine is matured in barrel, never in steel alone.

questions.q: In 1986 the Barry family bought a Watervale vineyard from Lindemans that gives the house its Riesling. Which vineyard?
questions.exp: Florita, once the source of Leo Buring's Rieslings, was bought from Lindemans in 1986; Springvale and Polish Hill are Grosset's sites, and McRae Wood is a Barry Shiraz.

report: The founder's birth year was not found: the reports of 2004 give his death that October at seventy nine, so the story gives his death and age rather than a pair of dates.
The Shiraz is dated 1968 by most accounts and 1969 by Decanter's obituary, so the record says the late 1960s; the vineyard's area is left out, as the accounts disagree and it is volatile.

The first The Armagh is the 1985 vintage in every source; Falstaff dates its launch to 1989 while another account speaks of it released in 1985, so the card and the story give Falstaff's 1989 for the launch and the checker may test it.
The 2016 vintage through La Place de Bordeaux in 2020 rests on two secondary accounts read through search summaries.

The Florita purchase of 1986 from Lindemans rests on Wine Business Magazine and a writer's article not cited by the house rule; the Florita trademark taken up by the family in 2004 is left out for want of a second source.
The founder's son and other members of the family are living and are not named. No swap proposed.

wine.name: Wendouree Shiraz
wine.grapes: Shiraz alone, from the estate's own vines.
wine.sites: The estate's own dry grown vineyard on clay at the southern end of the valley near Sevenhill, where the oldest Shiraz is told as planted in the 1890s and never grafted.
wine.making: Picked by hand and fermented in open, stainless steel lined fermenters with the cap plunged by hand, then pressed in an old basket press that runs on rails between the vats. The wine is matured in oak barrels, mostly seasoned, for about a year by one account, before it is bottled at the estate.
wine.glass: Blackberry, mulberry and satsuma plum over mint, liquorice and an iron note; dense and full, with high, firm, drying tannin and fresh acidity in youth, turning to leather and dried mint with age.
wine.ageing: Fierce and closed in youth, it is seldom ready before ten to fifteen years and lasts for decades.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for two hours or more, an old one gently off its sediment; a large red wine glass.

label.means: The estate's name, taken from Lake Wendouree at Ballarat in Victoria.
The geographical indication; at least 85 per cent of the wine must come from it.
The Australian name for Syrah, the one variety in this wine.

records.table: Wendouree Shiraz comes from dry grown vines near Sevenhill, some planted in the 1890s, made the old way in open vats and a basket press. It is dense and fiercely tannic when young, so keep it ten years and more and then decant it.
records.story: In the early 1890s a young man of the Birks family, who had grown up by Lake Wendouree at Ballarat in Victoria, planted vines with his brother near Sevenhill and named the estate for the lake. Accounts give 1892 or 1893 for the first vines, and the first Wendouree wines were released in 1895. Shiraz came first, then Cabernet Sauvignon, and Mataro and Malbec followed early in the twentieth century. In 1917 the founder handed the running of the estate to his son, who made its wine for decades, through years when few drinkers wanted dense dry red. The Birks family kept Wendouree until 1974, when it passed to a Sydney family who have changed very little: the vines are dry grown, the wine is made in open vats and a basket press, and nearly all of it is sold by letter to a mailing list. Because South Australia kept phylloxera out with its quarantine of 1899, the vines of the 1890s still stand on their own roots, and the house of Jim Barry says its Armagh Shiraz was planted from cuttings taken here. To a sommelier Wendouree Shiraz is old Clare in the glass: dense, tannic and slow.

others.name: Shiraz Malbec
others.note: An old Australian pairing of grapes the estate has kept alive.

others.name: Cabernet Malbec
others.note: Clare Cabernet Sauvignon given Malbec's colour and middle palate.

others.name: Shiraz Mataro
others.note: Shiraz with Mataro, the Australian name for Mourvèdre.

traps: Clare is known for Riesling, yet Wendouree makes only reds.
Wendouree is in the Clare Valley; Lake Wendouree, which gave it its name, is at Ballarat in Victoria.
Malbec has a long Australian history and is not solely an Argentine story.

cards.front: Wendouree: how is nearly all of its wine sold?
cards.back: By letter, to a mailing list.

cards.front: Which lake gave Wendouree its name, and why?

questions.q: A guest asks what makes Wendouree Shiraz feel like a wine of another century. Which part of its making fits?
opts: An old basket press on rails between open vats
A pneumatic press and sealed rotary fermenters
Long ageing in new American barriques
questions.exp: The wine is fermented in open vats with the cap plunged by hand and pressed in an old basket press; it sees mostly seasoned oak, not new American barrels.

questions.q: In which year did the Birks family let Wendouree pass to the family that has run it since?
questions.exp: The Birks family kept the estate until 1974; 1917 is the year the founder handed it to his son, and 1895 the year of the first wines.

report: Founded is left empty, as the library leaves it: accounts give 1892 and 1893 for the first vines and 1895 for the first wines, and the region record's 1895 is the year of the first release rather than of the founding.

The founder and his son are described rather than named, because their dates were not found in two sources; the buyers of 1974 are living and are not named, and Decanter tells the purchase as made by the father in law of the family that runs it, so the record says only that it passed to a Sydney family.
The library's holdings say ironstone and clay, and one secondary account says red clay over limestone; the record says clay alone.

The oak is told differently: one account says older French and American oak with no new oak, a retailer's sheet for 2018 says about a fifth new and about a year; the record says mostly seasoned, about a year by one account.
The stone cellars of 1914 and the Cabernet of 1898 rest on one source each and are left out.
The house has no web site to read; the facts rest on Decanter, Langton's and retailers' accounts. No swap proposed.

wine.name: Sevenhill St Ignatius
wine.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, about half, with Merlot, Malbec and Cabernet Franc for the rest.
wine.sites: Clare Valley fruit; the house's sheets read do not name the vineyards that give this blend.
wine.making: Each part is fermented on its skins for about twelve to fourteen days, by the house's own sheet, and the wine is then matured in French oak barrels, some new and some old, before it is blended and bottled at Sevenhill.
wine.glass: Blackberry and black olive over cassis, cedar and a touch of mint; medium in body and silky, with fine tannin and a dry, savoury finish.
wine.ageing: Approachable within a few years of the vintage, it keeps for ten years and more in a good year.
wine.serve: 15 to 17 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for an hour; a Bordeaux glass.

label.means: Named for Ignatius of Loyola, the founder of the Jesuit order that owns the winery.
The Jesuits' winery and the hamlet beside it, named for the seven hills of Rome.
The geographical indication; at least 85 per cent of the wine must come from it.

records.table: Sevenhill Cellars, the winery the Jesuits founded in 1851, names St Ignatius for the founder of their order. It is a Clare Valley blend of Cabernet Sauvignon with Merlot, Malbec and Cabernet Franc: blackberry and black olive, medium in body and silky.
records.story: In 1848 Jesuit priests reached Port Adelaide with Catholic migrants from German speaking Europe, where the revolutions of that year had driven the order out of many states. In 1851 they bought land near the village of Clare and named it Sevenhill for the seven hills of Rome, and, as the house tells it, planted the first vines that same year, so that the Church in the colony need not buy its altar wine from Europe. A Jesuit brother is remembered as the planter of those first vines, and wine followed within a few years, in 1856 by the house's account and in 1858 by others. Sacramental wine has been made at Sevenhill ever since, and the house sends it to churches across Asia and the Pacific. Table wine grew beside it: seven Jesuits in turn have held the post of winemaker, the seventh from 1972 until he retired in 2003, and the house's reserve Shiraz carries his name. In 2026 the winery marked its one hundred and seventy fifth year. Sevenhill calls itself the oldest winery of the Clare Valley and the last in Australia owned by the Jesuits. St Ignatius, a blend of four Bordeaux grapes named for the order's founder, shows the house as a maker of table wine as well as of wine for the altar.

others.name: Brother John May Reserve Shiraz
others.note: The house's reserve Shiraz, named for its seventh Jesuit winemaker, who retired in 2003.

others.name: Sacramental wine
others.note: Altar wine for the Church, the purpose for which the first vines were planted in 1851.

traps: Sevenhill names both the winery and the hamlet beside it, in the Clare Valley, not the Barossa.
St Ignatius is a blend of four Bordeaux grapes, not a Shiraz; the house's reserve Shiraz is a separate wine.

questions.exp: The vines were planted so the Church need not buy altar wine from Europe; sacramental wine has been made at Sevenhill ever since, beside its table wines.

report: Pick in doubt, answered: no source read calls St Ignatius the flagship. A retailer's note of 1997 calls it the top wine of the house's seventh Jesuit winemaker, and it is the long running signature red, but the Brother John May Reserve Shiraz now stands above it in the house's range. A swap to that wine may be weighed by the checker; the record keeps St Ignatius as the plan has it.
The blend's share is about half Cabernet Sauvignon, from one retailer's sheet for 2019 (52 per cent); the first vintage of St Ignatius and its time in oak were not found, so neither is given.
The sites are not named because no source read names the vineyards of this blend.

The first wine is given as 1856 by the house (five years after the vines) and 1858 by others, and the story says so; the first vines of 1851 rest on the house's history and the Southern Cross, and the plan's 1852 was not found.

The Jesuit brother who planted the first vines, the priest who led the Jesuits north and the seventh winemaker are described rather than named with dates, as two sources for their dates were not found; the seventh winemaker's years of 1972 to 2003 rest on the Jesuits' own notice and a secondary account, and one account dates his service from 1963.
The plan's why calls the founders Austrian Jesuits; the sources read say German speaking Europe and the revolutions of 1848, so the record says that. Not in WINE_PRODUCERS.

wine.name: Mount Horrocks Cordon Cut Riesling
wine.grapes: Riesling alone, from the house's own vines.
wine.sites: The house's Cordon Cut vineyard at Auburn, near the cellar door in the old railway station, planted wholly to Riesling in a warmer, lower part of the valley than its Watervale vines; in 2017, when frost struck Auburn, the fruit came from Watervale.
wine.making: Once the grapes are ripe the canes are cut, so the bunches, cut off from the vine's water, shrivel and concentrate on the vine for some weeks before they are picked. No botrytis is involved: the sweetness comes from the drying alone. The wine is sold in half bottles.
wine.glass: Lime marmalade and candied lemon peel over apricot and honey; sweet and concentrated, yet lifted by bright, firm acidity, so it finishes clean rather than heavy.
wine.ageing: Lovely young for its fresh lime, it keeps for ten years and more, turning towards marmalade and honey.
wine.serve: 6 to 8 degrees Celsius; no need to decant; a small white wine glass and a modest pour, with a fruit tart or blue cheese.

label.means: The method: the canes are cut so the ripe grapes dry and concentrate on the vine.
The geographical indication; at least 85 per cent of the wine must come from it.
The variety named on the label, here made sweet rather than dry.

records.table: Mount Horrocks Cordon Cut is a sweet Clare Valley Riesling made by cutting the canes once the grapes are ripe, so they dry and concentrate on the vine without botrytis. Lime marmalade and honey meet bright acidity; pour it cold, in a small glass.
records.story: The house takes its name from Mount Horrocks, which honours John Ainsworth Horrocks (1818 to 1846). Born at Penwortham Lodge in Lancashire, he founded the village of Penwortham in 1840, among the first European settlements of the Clare Valley, and he pioneered the use of camels in Australian exploration; in 1846, on an expedition to the north, his gun went off as his camel lurched, and he died of the wound. The wine house of his name was bought in 1993 by a winemaker who had sold fine wine in Perth, and in April 1998 the old railway station at Auburn was restored as its cellar door. The Cordon Cut vineyard lies close by, planted wholly to Riesling, and by 2014 the house counted more than twenty vintages of the wine. In 2000 the house was among the Clare makers who sealed their Riesling under screwcap together. The method gives the wine its name: once the grapes are ripe the canes are cut, and the fruit dries on the vine for weeks before picking. In 2012 the house's newsletter told of a Decanter trophy for its 2011. To a sommelier Cordon Cut is the valley's other face: a sweet Riesling from a region known for dry ones, sweet without noble rot.

others.name: Watervale Riesling
others.note: The house's dry Riesling from high Watervale vines, about 475 metres up on red loam over limestone.

traps: Cordon Cut is not a botrytis wine: the grapes dry on the vine after the canes are cut.
Mount Horrocks is named for John Ainsworth Horrocks, the pioneer of 1840, not for a family that owns the house.
Clare Riesling is mostly fully dry; Cordon Cut is the house's sweet wine, sold in half bottles.

cards.front: Mount Horrocks Cordon Cut: how do its grapes concentrate?
cards.back: The canes are cut once the grapes are ripe, and the fruit dries on the vine for weeks.

questions.q: A guest asks how Mount Horrocks Cordon Cut gains its sweetness. Which answer is right?
opts: Canes cut so the grapes dry on the vine
Noble rot encouraged by autumn mists
Grapes frozen after picking, before pressing
questions.exp: The canes are cut once the fruit is ripe and the grapes shrivel on the vine; no botrytis is involved, so the noble rot answer is the nearest wrong one.

questions.q: Mount Horrocks takes its name from a pioneer of the Clare Valley. Which village did he found in 1840?
questions.exp: John Ainsworth Horrocks founded Penwortham in 1840 and named it for his family's Lancashire home; Sevenhill was the Jesuits' foundation of 1851.

report: Founded is left empty: 1982 is given by two web pages of little standing (a wine directory and a wine wiki), and one of them names founders the house's own pages do not; the house's pages read tell only the purchase of 1993.
The first vintage of Cordon Cut was not found; the house's newsletter of 2014 counts more than twenty vintages, so the story says that.
The owner since 1993 is living and is not named; the story speaks of the purchase as history.

The house's place among the fourteen screwcap producers of 2000 rests on secondary accounts read through search summaries, with the Clare Valley Wine and Grape Association's page giving the fourteen but not, in the summary read, their names; the checker may test it or cut the sentence.
Horrocks's dates, Penwortham of 1840 and the camel rest on the Australian Dictionary of Biography and Wikipedia.

The plan calls it a Watervale house; its cellar door and the Cordon Cut vineyard are at Auburn and its dry Riesling vines at Watervale, so the place is Auburn. The plan's why says the canes are cut so the fruit dries on the vine, which the record keeps. No swap proposed.
